paras: The Atlanta messenger boys' attacks on Black telegraph messengers took place in Atlanta, Georgia, on June 27 and 28, 1903, when white messenger boys discharged by the Western Union and Postal Telegraph companies beat and stoned the Black men hired to replace them. Several messengers were reported badly bruised or hurt, and police repeatedly scattered the boys, but no deaths or arrests were reported. New York papers carried the story as a messenger boys' "riot," while Black weeklies reprinted it as evidence that Black workers were winning employers' confidence.

On the afternoon of Saturday, June 27, the two telegraph companies in Atlanta put about 200 white messenger boys out of work and filled their places with Black men. Company officials said the change was made to get better service, and the Sun added that the boys had refused to wear the uniform. According to the Sun's Atlanta correspondent, the companies hired grown men rather than Black boys because "it was well known that the white boys would not be long in running them off the streets."

Fighting broke out around the telegraph headquarters the same night, as the discharged boys banded together and attacked the new messengers whenever they left the office. At Western Union headquarters six boys jumped on one man and "bruised him badly" before the office force rescued him, and the management called the police to clear the boys from the office. The boys stayed nearby and said they would keep attacking the messengers until the companies took them back.

On Sunday, June 28, the attacks spread into the streets, where boys in gangs of eight and ten waited for any Black messenger carrying a telegram. The messengers spent the day and evening dodging stones and rocks, and the Tribune's dispatch said several were badly hurt by rocks while others were bruised in fights. Police scattered the crowds at the telegraph offices several times, but the boys moved out to meet the messengers in what the Sun called "guerrilla warfare." They told reporters they would never allow the Black messengers to keep their places.

None of the dispatches names a victim or reports an arrest, and no report of later violence was found. Writing on July 1, the Savannah Morning News said the companies called the change "purely a business matter" and planned to keep some boys with good records in their offices.

The fullest accounts appeared in New York, where the Sun ran Atlanta dispatches on June 28 and 29 under the headlines "MESSENGER' BOYS RIOT" and "FIGHT NEGRO MESSENGERS," and the Tribune ran "HARD TIME FOR NEGRO MESSENGERS." These dispatches described the attacks as the boys' "day of revenge" and made no comment on the victims. Elsewhere white coverage dropped the violence entirely: the Savannah Morning News, one-line briefs in Iowa and North Dakota, and a New Haven editorial reported only that Black men had replaced the boys. The New Haven editorial treated the firing as no "large compliment" to young white Southerners.

The Black press took the story from the Chicago Monitor, whose text the Wisconsin Weekly Advocate ran on July 9 under "Mob Negro Messenger Boys," and the Wichita Searchlight repeated it on July 25. That version reported that "riots" followed and that every colored messenger leaving the office was attacked, then added that Atlanta's Black messengers, like Chicago's, were giving service that commended them to employers, "prejudice to the contrary notwithstanding." The Professional World printed a shorter "Atlanta, special" version on July 10 without comment. Where the white dispatches dwelt on the boys' grievance and their "warfare," the Black papers presented the episode chiefly as a sign of Black workers' advance in the face of white hostility.

bases: Discharged white messenger boys attacked the Black men hired in their places, saying they would force the companies to take them back and never allow the Black messengers to keep the jobs (A1, A3).

Two separate New York papers (A2, A3) carry differently worded Atlanta dispatches of June 28 describing the stoning, and the Sun's June 27 dispatch (A1) and the Black-press version (A7, A8) independently describe attacks on messengers leaving the offices.

accounts.label: New York Sun Atlanta dispatch, June 27
accounts.gist: The boys banded together and a mob of them attacked the messengers each time they left the office; six boys beat one man before the office force rescued him, and the police cleared the office.

accounts.label: Atlanta dispatches, June 28 (Sun and Tribune)
accounts.gist: Gangs of boys lurked in the streets and stoned or assaulted any Black messenger carrying a telegram; several were badly hurt and the police repeatedly scattered the boys.

accounts.label: Black-press version (Chicago Monitor, 'Atlanta, special')
accounts.gist: Riots followed around the telegraph offices and every colored messenger leaving was attacked by the white boys; the Monitor added that the hiring showed Black messengers' service commended them to employers.

accounts.label: Companies' statement
accounts.gist: The companies said the change was a business matter, made for better service because the boys would not do the work properly or wear the uniform.

framing.detail: The Sun headlined 'MESSENGER' BOYS RIOT.' and 'Discharged Telegraph Boys in Atlanta Have a Riotous Sunday,' calling the attacks the boys' 'day of revenge' and 'guerrilla warfare' without comment on the victims.
The Tribune headlined 'HARD TIME FOR NEGRO MESSENGERS,' writing from the messengers' side of the stoning.
Georgia's Savannah Morning News, the Iowa and North Dakota briefs, and a New Haven editorial reported only the replacement of the boys, not the attacks.

Under 'Mob Negro Messenger Boys' the Chicago Monitor text, reprinted in Milwaukee and Wichita, called the change evidence of good Black service 'prejudice to the contrary notwithstanding' and wished 'Success to the young colored American.'
